\chapter{The Tree}
\label{ch:te-tree}
\hlchaptermodality{54}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a tree and its parts in Telugu, from the seed it started as to the branch at the top.}

Complete TE-C54-seedling and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[ceṭṭu]{\te{చెట్టు} (ceṭṭu) — a tree}

\label{lesson:TE-C54-tree}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mabbu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చెట్టు}}
\textbf{\te{చెట్టు}} (\emph{ceṭṭu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.

\te{చెట్టు} is inherited and old. The Dravidian family kept the shape but shuffled the meaning: Tamil's \emph{ceṭi} is a bush or a shrub, a small woody thing, while Telugu raised the same word to the full-grown tree and left the bush to other words.

A meaning that moves up or down the scale like that is the commonest kind of drift there is. The word holds its place in the family; what it points at slides.

\te{మ్రాను} is another Telugu word for a tree, older-sounding and now mostly literary. \te{చెట్టు} is what anybody says.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The thing the rest of this chapter is made of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ceṭṭu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ceṭṭu}, then \emph{puvvu}, and say which one grows on the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చెట్టు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[komma]{\te{కొమ్మ} (komma) — a branch}

\label{lesson:TE-C54-branch}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ceṭṭu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కొమ్మ}}
\textbf{\te{కొమ్మ}} (\emph{komma}) — \textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కొమ్మ} is the branch, the arm the \te{చెట్టు} puts out sideways.

It stands very close to \te{కొమ్ము}, the horn of an animal, and the closeness is not an accident: both are the thing that grows out and forks. A tree wearing horns is a fair description of a tree in winter.

\te{కొమ్మ} turns up in old poetry meaning a young woman, by way of the slenderness of a branch. That sense has gone quiet, but it is why the word looks odd inside a love poem.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the tree and what it puts out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{komma}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{komma}, then \emph{ceṭṭu}, and say which is part of which
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కొమ్మ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vēru]{\te{వేరు} (vēru) — a root}

\label{lesson:TE-C54-root}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{komma} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వేరు}}
\textbf{\te{వేరు}} (\emph{vēru}) — \textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.

\te{వేరు} is the root under the \te{చెట్టు}. It also means \textquotedblleft{}separate, apart, other\textquotedblright{} — \te{వేరు} as an answer means \textquotedblleft{}that is a different thing\textquotedblright{}.

One shape, two jobs, and they are not far apart when you think about what a root does: it is the part that is set aside, buried, kept out of the daylight and out of the reckoning.

Telugu is comfortable letting a word carry a solid thing and an abstract idea at once. You had one working two jobs a moment ago, with \te{చుక్క}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: what is up, what is out, and what is under.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vēru}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vēru}, then \emph{komma}, and say which end of the \te{చెట్టు} each one is at
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{వేరు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vittanaṁ]{\te{విత్తనం} (vittanaṁ) — a seed}

\label{lesson:TE-C54-seed}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vēru} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{విత్తనం}}
\textbf{\te{విత్తనం}} (\emph{vittanaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.

\te{విత్తనం} is the seed, and it is built on \te{విత్తు}, \textquotedblleft{}to sow\textquotedblright{}. The word for the thing comes out of the word for the act, which is the ordinary direction of travel: people had been sowing for a long time before anybody needed a name for what they held.

Sanskrit's \emph{bīja} was borrowed in as \emph{bījaṁ}, and it does the abstract work — the seed of an idea, the germ of a quarrel. \te{విత్తనం} stays in the sack.

The whole chapter is inside this word. A \te{విత్తనం} becomes a \te{చెట్టు} with a \te{వేరు} below and a \te{కొమ్మ} above.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vittanaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vittanaṁ}, then \emph{ceṭṭu}, and say which one comes first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{విత్తనం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mokka]{\te{మొక్క} (mokka) — a young plant}

\label{lesson:TE-C54-seedling}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vittanaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మొక్క}}
\textbf{\te{మొక్క}} (\emph{mokka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a young plant\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మొక్క} is what the \te{విత్తనం} becomes before it earns the name \te{చెట్టు}: a seedling, a sapling, anything small and green and rooted.

The line between \te{మొక్క} and \te{చెట్టు} is about woodiness rather than height. A tomato plant stays a \te{మొక్క} at any size, because it stays soft. A \te{చెట్టు} has bark.

Do not tie it to \te{మొక్కు}, \textquotedblleft{}to bow, to make a vow\textquotedblright{}, which sounds close. Telugu has a good many pairs like that, and a resemblance on its own settles nothing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{చెట్టు}, \te{కొమ్మ}, \te{వేరు}, \te{విత్తనం}, \te{మొక్క}. A tree, its parts, and its beginning.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mokka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say them again as a life story, starting with the seed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మొక్క} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a young plant\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
